practice1.prompt: let each mistake raise the error that names it

cases.name: the errors are let out, not caught
cases.describe: no try/except around either function, so the error can name itself

hiddenCases.name: a total that is text raises TypeError

practice1.hint: Both functions are one line. The temptation is to guard against the bad case -- a missing name, zero people -- but a guard replaces an error you can read with a wrong answer you cannot. This exercise wants the error.

questions.prompt: Match each mistake to the error Python raises for it.
left: Looking up a key that is not in the dictionary
Adding a string to a number
Using a variable that was never assigned
questions.explain: The name of the error is the first real clue you get. Knowing which mistake produces which name turns a red block of text into a starting point.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a SyntaxError and the errors above?
choices: A SyntaxError stops the file before any of it runs
A SyntaxError only happens in functions
A SyntaxError can be caught with except
questions.explain: Python parses the whole file before running a line of it, so a SyntaxError means nothing ran at all. The others happen partway through, with some work already done.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a guard for a missing dictionary key sometimes make debugging harder?
choices: It replaces a KeyError that names the problem with a wrong answer that hides it
questions.explain: A guard is right when you know what the missing case should do. Added early, before you know, it converts a loud failure into a quiet wrong answer that surfaces somewhere else entirely.

questions.prompt: Which of these raise a TypeError?
questions.explain: TypeError is Python saying the operation is fine but these types cannot do it. Dividing two numbers is the one case here where the types match the operation.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Three kinds, and the useful distinction is when each one is discovered: before anything runs, partway through, or not at all until you check the answer.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Name the errors themselves, then say what causes each one. Handling comes after knowing what you are handling.
